berlin-airlift.title: The Berlin Airlift, 1948–49
berlin-airlift.note: A schematic eight hours. Aircraft flew in by the northern and southern corridors and out by the central one, every few minutes, around the clock. Each figure stands for a stream of aircraft.

markers.label: West Berlin needs about 4,500 tonnes a day

captions.text: June 1948. The Soviet Union has closed every road, railway and canal into West Berlin. Only three air corridors, each 32 km wide, are guaranteed by treaty.
American C-54s from Rhein-Main and Wiesbaden fly in by the southern corridor. Aircraft from bases in the British zone use the northern one.
They land at Tempelhof and Gatow, unload in minutes, and leave by the central corridor. Pilots who missed a landing had to fly home with their load and start again.
In November 1948 a third airfield opens at Tegel, built in 90 days by about 19,000 Berliners, many of them women.
On 16 April 1949, the Easter Parade, crews land 12,941 tonnes in 24 hours: one aircraft about every minute. Stalin lifts the blockade on 12 May.

fall-of-saigon.title: The fall of South Vietnam, March – April 1975
fall-of-saigon.note: Schematic. Corps and divisions are shown as single blocks; positions and dates are approximate. The supply route follows modern roads through Laos close to the old trail.

markers.label: 14 Mar: Thieu orders the Highlands abandoned
9–21 Apr: last stand at Xuan Loc
30 Apr: tanks enter the presidential palace

captions.text: March 1975. The Americans have gone. Down the Ho Chi Minh Trail, now a network of all-weather roads and fuel pipelines, North Vietnam has built up its forces for an offensive it expects to take two years.
10 March: North Vietnamese divisions take Ban Me Thuot in the Central Highlands.
President Thieu orders the Highlands abandoned. The retreat to the coast turns into a rout. Tens of thousands of soldiers and civilians die on Route 7B.
In the north, panic spreads. Hue falls on 25 March and Da Nang on 29 March, as crowds fight for places on the last planes and boats.
Hanoi orders its army to take Saigon before the May rains. Divisions race down the coast road.
At Xuan Loc, 60 km from Saigon, the ARVN 18th Division holds for twelve days. On 21 April the town falls and Thieu resigns.
Sixteen North Vietnamese divisions close in on Saigon from every side.
29 April: Operation Frequent Wind. US helicopters lift about 7,000 Americans and Vietnamese from the city to ships offshore. Many thousands who had worked with the Americans are left behind.
30 April, late morning: a tank crashes through the palace gates and South Vietnam surrenders.
